faq.a: MCH helps classify the type of anaemia (microcytic‑hypochromic vs macrocytic), guiding the next diagnostic step.
faq.q: Why is MCH useful if I already have haemoglobin level?

faq.a: Acute malaria usually causes low MCH via haemolysis and iron loss; high MCH would point to a co‑existing folate deficiency.
faq.q: Can malaria cause a high MCH?
What if the laboratory cannot calculate MCH?

exam: A 28‑year‑old woman with heavy menstrual bleeding has Hb 9 g/dL, MCV 70 fL, MCH 22 pg. What is the most likely diagnosis and next investigation? — Microcytic hypochromic anaemia; order serum ferritin or iron studies.
A patient with HIV presents with Hb 8 g/dL, MCH 30 pg, MCV 105 fL. Which deficiency should you suspect and why? — Folate or B12 deficiency; high MCH with macrocytosis suggests megaloblastic anaemia.

In a malaria‑endemic clinic, a child’s CBC shows low Hb, low MCH, and high RDW. What are the two most probable causes? — Iron deficiency from chronic blood loss and malaria‑induced haemolysis; investigate stool for hookworm and do malaria rapid test.

You receive a CBC with normal MCH but low MCV. How do you interpret this discordance? — Consider mixed anaemia (iron deficiency plus thalassaemia trait) or laboratory error; review peripheral smear and repeat test.

A pregnant woman at 20 weeks has Hb 10 g/dL, MCH 28 pg, but complains of numbness in feet. What is your priority? — Evaluate for vitamin B12 deficiency despite normal MCH; order B12 level and start supplementation if low.

A patient with severe anaemia (Hb 6 g/dL) is haemodynamically stable. Do you transfuse immediately? Why or why not? — No, unless there are signs of cardiac compromise; treat underlying cause and monitor, reserving transfusion for instability.

How does chronic kidney disease affect MCH and what is the management implication? — CKD often causes normochromic normocytic anaemia (normal MCH); treat with erythropoiesis‑stimulating agents and iron supplementation.

A lab reports MCH 35 pg in a patient on chronic antimalarial prophylaxis. What drug effect could explain this? — Primaquine can cause hemolysis with reticulocytosis, raising MCH; assess for hemolysis and consider alternative prophylaxis.
ai.title: Mean Corpuscular Hemoglobin (MCH)
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: MCH measures the average amount of hemoglobin per red cell, helping to classify anaemia. It is calculated from CBC values and guides further work‑up, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Normal range: 27–33 pg (varies slightly by laboratory).
Low MCH = hypochromic anaemia; high MCH = macrocytic or hyperchromic states.
sections.p: MCH is the average mass of hemoglobin contained in a single erythrocyte, expressed in picograms (pg). It is derived from the complete blood count (CBC) using the formula: MCH = (Hb × 10) / RBC.

b: Mild anaemia: Hb 10–11 g/dL, MCH often low‑normal.
Moderate anaemia: Hb 8–9.9 g/dL, MCH usually low.
Severe anaemia: Hb <8 g/dL, MCH markedly low.
sections.p: MCH itself is not staged, but it contributes to anaemia severity grading together with haemoglobin level.

b: Low MCH (hypochromic): iron deficiency, chronic blood loss, hookworm, malaria, TB, HIV‑associated anaemia, thalassaemia trait.
High MCH (hyperchromic): folate or vitamin B12 deficiency, megaloblastic anaemia, liver disease, hypothyroidism, reticulocytosis after haemolysis.
sections.p: Interpret MCH in the context of red cell indices (MCV, RDW) and clinical setting.

b: Pallor of conjunctivae and nail beds.
Tachycardia, low‑output symptoms if severe.
sections.p: Patients present with symptoms of anaemia—fatigue, dyspnoea on exertion, pallor—and may have signs specific to the underlying cause (e.g., koilonychia in iron deficiency, glossitis in B12 deficiency).
Use a stepwise approach: CBC → iron studies → vitamin levels → infection screens where relevant.

t.b: What type of anaemia? Low MCH with low MCV points to microcytic hypochromic anaemia.

t.a: Serum ferritin / iron / total iron‑binding capacity
t.b: Is iron deficiency present? Low ferritin confirms iron deficiency; if unavailable, use transferrin saturation or peripheral smear clues.
Is a macrocytic cause likely? Low B12 or folate explains high MCH with high MCV.

t.a: Stool occult blood or helminth microscopy
t.b: Is chronic blood loss or hookworm infection causing iron loss? Positive test supports iron‑deficiency work‑up.

t.a: HIV or TB screening (rapid test, GeneXpert)
t.b: Is a chronic infection driving anaemia? Positive test directs disease‑specific therapy.

b: Hb <7 g/dL with tachycardia, hypotension, or chest pain.
Neurological deficits in B12 deficiency (paresthesiae, gait disturbance).
sections.p: Severe anaemia can precipitate cardiac failure, ischemic chest pain, or acute decompensation in pregnancy.

b: Infection‑related anaemia: treat HIV, TB, malaria, or schistosomiasis per national guidelines.
Severe anaemia: consider blood transfusion if haemodynamic instability; avoid transfusion in stable patients to limit risk.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first; provide supportive therapy while monitoring haemoglobin and MCH trends.

b: Iron therapy: repeat CBC and ferritin after 4 weeks; continue for 3 months beyond normalisation.
B12/folate: repeat CBC after 6 weeks; monitor neurologic recovery in B12 deficiency.
Educate on dietary sources (meat, legumes, leafy greens) and deworming.
sections.p: Re‑check CBC after 2–4 weeks of therapy; ensure MCH normalises with correction of the primary defect.

b: MCHC reflects haemoglobin concentration per cell volume; low MCHC = hypochromia, but normal MCH can coexist.
MCV measures cell size; macrocytosis with high MCH suggests megaloblastic anaemia.
sections.p: MCH is sometimes mixed up with MCHC (mean corpuscular haemoglobin concentration) or MCV.

b: Concurrent iron deficiency and haemolysis may give a near‑normal MCH; look at RDW and smear.
Laboratory error: poor sample handling can falsely lower MCH.
sections.p: MCH can appear normal in mixed anaemias or when reticulocytosis raises MCH artificially.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden drop in haemoglobin with chest pain or syncope
